q: The House With Owls (1907) and Tolstoy House (1912) represent National Romanticism in which country?
n: Both are Russian examples, fitting the style's spread mainly to St. Petersburg.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of Metabolists?
n: Tadao Ando appears on the futurist list, not the Metabolist one. The Metabolists listed are Tange, Kurokawa, Safdie, Kikutake, and Jonas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: How did National Romanticism differ from nostalgic Gothic Revival elsewhere?
o: It used reformed housing design to carry forward-looking social and political aims
It was used only for churches
n: Unlike nostalgic Gothic Revival, National Romanticism carried progressive social and political ideals through reformed housing.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Bergen Station (1913), Frogner Church (1907), and the Norwegian Institute of Technology (1910) are National Romantic examples from which country?
n: All three are Norwegian, along with Vålerenga Church (1902).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Monumentalism is based on which notion?
o: That ornament must express the region's craft
That a building should be demolished when its use ends
That form should change with every new technology
That an object's form should last, and some forms have external validity
n: Monumentalism holds that form should last and that some forms carry external validity, expressed through construction on a grand scale.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Monumentalism

q: Among the many ideas behind Metabolism, which two does the table name?
n: Marxist theories and biological processes are the influences named; they fit a movement about cities that grow.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Which of these is NOT one of the Swedish National Romantic examples?
n: Copenhagen City Hall is in Denmark. The Swedish examples are the Church of the Epiphany, Stockholm Court House, Röhsska Museum, and Stockholm City Hall.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Where did Metabolism have its first international exposure?
o: The 1988 MoMA exhibit in New York
n: Metabolism first reached an international audience at CIAM's 1959 meeting. Osaka 1970 is where the most Metabolist work was built.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: After the 1973 oil crisis, where did the Metabolists turn their attention?
n: After the 1973 oil crisis they looked away from Japan, toward Africa and the Middle East.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Apart from a few buildings, what became of the Metabolists' large proposals?
o: They were rebuilt after the 1973 oil crisis
They were built across Tokyo in the 1960s
They were adopted as national housing policy
n: Although the 1960 conference gave them international exposure, their ideas remained largely theoretical; only smaller individual buildings were built.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Which title was NOT one of the four essays in the Metabolism manifesto?
n: The four essays were Ocean City, Space City, Towards Group Form, and Material and Man. 'Plug-in City' is a British Archigram project, though the Metabolists also imagined plug-in capsule towers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Metabolist ideas were tentatively tested by students from whose studio?
n: Students from Kenzo Tange's MIT studio tested the ideas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Which of these National Romantic buildings is a Finnish example?
n: The Finnish National Theatre (1902) and the National Museum of Finland (1905) are the Finnish examples. Vålerenga Church is Norwegian, Copenhagen City Hall Danish, and Röhsska Museum Swedish.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Tarvaspää (1913, Finland), a National Romantic example, was built as the house and studio of whom?
n: Tarvaspää was built by and for Finnish painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela. Tolstoy's name belongs to Tolstoy House, the Russian example.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Which built work by Kisho Kurokawa applied Metabolist principles?
n: Kurokawa built the Nakagin Capsule Tower. The Yamanashi Press and Broadcaster Centre is Kenzo Tange's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: The greatest concentration of Metabolist work was found at which event, master-planned by Kenzo Tange?
n: Tange master-planned the 1970 Osaka World Exposition, where Kikutake and Kurokawa designed pavilions.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Metabolism, a post-war Japanese movement, fused ideas about megastructures with what?
n: Metabolism combined megastructures with organic biological growth, imagining cities that could grow and change like living things.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Which group of young architects prepared the Metabolism manifesto?
o: Kiyonori Kikutake, Kisho Kurokawa, and Fumihiko Maki
Kenzo Tange, Tadao Ando, and Toyo Ito
Arata Isozaki, Kazuo Shinohara, and Kenzo Tange
Moshe Safdie, Walter Jonas, and Kenzo Tange
n: Kikutake, Kurokawa, and Maki prepared the manifesto. Tange was the mentor figure whose MIT students tested the ideas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Which building is Denmark's National Romantic example in the table?
n: Copenhagen City Hall (1905) is the Danish example. Stockholm City Hall is the Swedish one, and it also appears among revivalist buildings as "Medieval".
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: National Romantic designers turned to early Medieval and even prehistoric precedents. What drove this choice?
o: A search for cheap local materials
"Dream of the North" nationalism and a reaction to industrialism
n: They wanted a style fitting the character of a people, reacting against industrialism and driven by "Dream of the North" nationalism and renewed interest in the eddas and sagas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of Monumentalists?
n: Aalto is listed with the functionalists and organic architects. The monumentalists are Schinkel, Behrens, Poelzig, Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier, T. Garnier, and A. Perret.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Monumentalism

q: The National Romantic style, part of a late-19th and early-20th-century movement, came from which region, and how is it often classified?
o: Central Europe; often considered a form of Baroque
The Nordic countries; often considered a form of Art Nouveau
The British Isles; often considered a form of Gothic Revival
Russia; often considered a form of Constructivism
n: National Romanticism was a Nordic style, often considered a form of Art Nouveau.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: The National Romantic style spread across Finland and the Scandinavian countries and into which other country, mainly its city of St. Petersburg?
n: Besides Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, it reached Russia, mainly St. Petersburg.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: National Romanticism

q: The Metabolism manifesto was prepared for which event?
n: Kiyonori Kikutake, Kisho Kurokawa, and Fumihiko Maki prepared the manifesto during preparations for the 1960 Tokyo World Design Conference.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Metabolism

q: Used loosely, 'eclecticism' covers the mix of 1800s styles that followed Neo-classicism. From roughly which year?
n: It is applied to 19th-century variety after Neo-classicism, from about 1820.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: What gap in Sullivan's credo does the apartment-building example expose?
o: It ignores the cost of construction
It does not say whose function is meant; owners and tenants may want different things
It does not apply to buildings over ten storeys
It forbids the use of new materials
n: The credo never says whose function counts. An apartment architect may be at odds with the owners over look and feel, and with future tenants too.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Since the 1970s, the 19th-century revivals once called eclectic have generally been referred to as aspects of what?
n: Those revivals are now generally treated as aspects of historicism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: In academic criticism, 'functionalism' was used as a synonym for 'gauche' when describing whose work?
o: Mies van der Rohe's glass towers
n: Buckminster Fuller's geodesic domes are the example of 'functionalism' used to mean 'gauche'.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of functionalists?
n: Hugo Häring is listed with the expressionists and organic architects. Aalto, Bryggman, and Ekelund are on the functionalist list, along with Blomstedt, Huttunen, Ullberg, and Ypya.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Functionalism holds that architects should design a building based on what?
o: The historical style of its region
The personal taste of the client
n: Functionalism bases design on the building's purpose. The table warns this is less self-evident than it sounds and has caused confusion and controversy.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: From the mid-1930s, functionalism was confused with what, until it became a term of criticism?
n: Functionalism was conflated with a lack of ornament and became a pejorative for bald, brutal ways of covering space, like cheap commercial buildings and sheds.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Which building does the table cite as a notable example of eclecticism, merging oriental motifs with forms from the natural world?
n: Gaudí's Sagrada Família is the eclectic example. It was designed at the eclectic peak (1883–1926) and is still under construction.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: Which of Louis Sullivan's protégés is also cited as an exemplar of functional design?
n: Frank Lloyd Wright, Sullivan's protégé, is cited as a functional designer. Adler was Sullivan's partner, not his protégé.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Eclecticism, a 19th- and 20th-century style, is defined by what?
o: Strict loyalty to a single historical style
Mixing elements of earlier styles in one work to create something new
Growing the building from its natural site
n: Eclecticism combines elements from several earlier styles in a single work to make something new and original. Strict loyalty to one style is revivalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: In which countries did Functionalism have its strongest influence?
o: Germany, Czechoslovakia, the USSR, and the Netherlands
The United States, Canada, Britain, and Australia
n: Its strongest influence was in Germany, Czechoslovakia, the USSR, and the Netherlands. The Nordic option is tempting because the listed functionalist architects are Finnish.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: How does the table define Defunctionalism?
o: A return to Sullivan's original credo
A style that ignores the classic approach, disregarding functionalisms that have failed
The removal of services from view
n: Defunctionalism ignores the classic approach to design and disregards the functionalisms that failed in many instances.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Defunctionalism

q: According to Sullivan's credo, what happens once a building's functional aspects are satisfied?
o: Ornament must then be added to make it beautiful
Architectural beauty follows naturally and necessarily
The building can be copied for other uses
n: Sullivan held that size, massing, and spatial grammar should follow function alone, and that beauty would then follow naturally.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Who coined the phrase 'form ever follows function', and in what year?
n: Chicago architect Louis Sullivan coined the phrase in 1896. Frank Lloyd Wright was his protégé, not the author.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: In eclectic architecture and interiors, how are the mixed elements chosen?
o: By their suitability to the project and overall aesthetic value
By the national origin of the client
n: Structural features, furniture, motifs, historical ornament, and foreign cultural motifs are picked for suitability and aesthetic value.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: Why is Sullivan's 'form follows function' credo often seen as ironic?
o: Because he never designed a tall building
Because he used intricate ornament extensively
Because he later wrote against functionalism
n: Functionalists commonly believe ornament serves no function, yet Sullivan was famous for his intricate ornament.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Functionalism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of eclectic architects?
n: Gropius is a modernist. The eclectic list includes Burnham, Alexander Jackson Davis, Gaudí, Hunt, McKim, Mead, Shaw, and White.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Eclecticism

q: Later redefinitions extended the term 'Expressionist architecture' back to which year?
n: Subsequent redefinitions pushed it back to 1905. Today it can describe architecture of any date showing distortion, fragmentation, or violent emotion.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Which of these architects appears on the table's list of futurist architects?
n: Oscar Niemeyer is on the futurist list, along with names such as Tadao Ando, Santiago Calatrava, Zaha Hadid, and Eero Saarinen. Shaw is on the eclectic list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Expressionists took inspiration from crystals, rock formations, caves, peaks, and lightning. This makes their work more mineral and elemental than which style?
n: Expressionism is described as more mineral and elemental than florid and organic Art Nouveau, even though the two are close in time.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Expressionism took advantage of the technical possibilities of which mass-produced materials?
n: Mass-produced brick, steel, and especially glass are named. Raw concrete with exposed aggregate is Brutalist.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Expressionist architecture developed alongside the expressionist visual and performing arts and dominated especially in which country?
n: Expressionism developed across Europe but especially dominated in Germany.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Which artist is NOT named among those Futurism attracted?
n: Mondrian belongs to De Stijl. Boccioni, Balla, Depero, and Prampolini are the futurist artists named.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Which futurist architect, though he built little, translated the futurist vision into urban form?
n: Antonio Sant'Elia turned the futurist vision into urban designs. Marchi is on the table's futurist architects list but is not the one credited with this.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Walter Gropius appears on the expressionist list with what qualification?
o: As a critic, not a designer
n: Gropius is listed as expressionist for his early period only, before the Bauhaus moved toward plain functional design.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: What date range does the isms table give for Expressionism?
n: The isms table dates Expressionism 1910 to 1930. The movements table on page 3 ends it at 1925, so the two tables differ.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Futurism was founded by which poet, whose manifesto appeared in 1909?
n: Marinetti founded Futurism and wrote the Manifesto of Futurism in 1909. Boccioni was an artist member, and Sant'Elia the architect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Which themes did the Futurists hold up?
o: Harmony with nature and sustainable growth
A return to rural craft and village life
Worship of machines and a celebration of war and violence
n: Futurists celebrated the machine age and glorified war and violence; several prominent futurists were killed after volunteering in World War I.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Which trait of Expressionism describes its treatment of realism?
o: Realism was subordinated to symbolic or stylistic expression of inner experience
Realism was abandoned in favour of machine efficiency
Realism was achieved through photographic detail
Realism was pursued through exact historical copying
n: Expressionism put symbolic expression of inner experience above realism, and distorted form for emotional effect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Why did Expressionism produce so many works on paper and models?
o: Because discovering and representing concepts mattered more than finished products
Because building materials were banned in wartime
Because the architects were mostly painters
n: Expressionists valued discovering and representing concepts over pragmatic finished buildings, so much of their work stayed on paper. Distortion of form for emotional effect is another listed trait.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: The term 'Expressionist architecture' first described the avant-garde of which countries, from 1910 until 1930?
o: German, Dutch, Austrian, Czech, and Danish
n: It first described the German, Dutch, Austrian, Czech, and Danish avant-garde. Later uses widened it to the rest of Europe.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Futurist architecture, born in Italy, is characterised by what?
o: Strong chromaticism and long dynamic lines suggesting speed and motion
Austere right angles and primary colours
Heavy stone masses and small windows
Ornament of undulating flowers and stalks
n: Futurism used strong colour and long dynamic lines suggesting speed, motion, urgency, and lyricism. Right angles and primary colours are De Stijl.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Expressionist architecture leans more toward which historical styles than toward the classical?
n: It tends toward the Gothic rather than the classical, and toward the Romanesque and rococo. It also uses artisan craftsmanship.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: In what year did Marinetti publish the Manifesto of Futurism?
n: The manifesto appeared in 1909. 1917 is the founding of De Stijl, and 1928 the founding of CIAM.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Futurism

q: Which architect is NOT on the isms table's list of expressionists?
n: Alvar Aalto is listed under Functionalism and organic architecture. Finsterlin, Krayl, and Kramer are expressionists.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: Expressionism is said to be as eastern as western. Which sources does it draw on as much as Roman or Greek?
n: Expressionism draws on Moorish, Islamic, Egyptian, and Indian art and architecture, and conceives architecture as a work of art.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 8 — Architectural Isms: Expressionism

q: In his statement on organic architecture, how did Wright say form should be determined?
o: By the historic style of the region
By way of the nature of materials
By the wishes of the client
By the rules of the classical orders
n: Wright rejected fixed forms from past, present, or future and asked for form determined by the nature of materials.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: Fallingwater, Wright's well-known organic house for the Kaufmann family in rural Pennsylvania, is placed where on its site?
o: On a hilltop overlooking the waterfall
Directly over the waterfall and creek
Beside the waterfall, facing away from it
Across the valley from the creek
n: Wright put the house directly over the waterfall and creek, with stone striations and beige concrete cantilevers echoing the rock ledges.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: Which three architects were among the principal members of De Stijl?
o: Gerrit Rietveld, Robert van 't Hoff, and J.J.P. Oud
Michel de Klerk, Piet Kramer, and Jan Wils
Mies van der Rohe, Gropius, and Meyer
n: Rietveld, van 't Hoff, and Oud were the architect members. De Klerk and Kramer were Amsterdam School expressionists.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: Besides the movement, 'De Stijl' was also the name of a journal published by whom?
n: Theo van Doesburg, painter, designer, writer, and critic, published the journal to spread the group's theories.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of Neo-Plasticism architects?
n: Michel de Klerk is an expressionist. The Neo-Plasticism architects are van Eesteren, van 't Hoff, Kiesler, Oud, Rietveld, and Wils.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of organic architects?
n: Philip Johnson is associated with the International Style and Deconstructivism. Hundertwasser, Makovecz, and Toyo Ito are on the organic list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: According to Mondrian, the new plastic idea should express itself through what?
o: The straight line and clearly defined primary colour
n: Mondrian wrote that it should ignore the particulars of appearance and find expression in the straight line and clearly defined primary colour.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: To what did De Stijl reduce visual composition?
o: Curves and spirals in earth tones
Floral forms in gold and green
Vertical and horizontal directions, using primary colours with black and white
n: De Stijl pursued pure abstraction through vertical and horizontal lines and only primary colours plus black and white.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: Which painter was NOT among De Stijl's principal members?
n: Kandinsky taught at the Bauhaus. The principal De Stijl painters were Mondrian, Huszár, and van der Leck.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: How is organic architecture expressed in Wright's design process?
o: Each room is designed in a different historical style
Materials, motifs, and ordering principles repeat so every element, down to windows and chairs, relates to the whole
Only the exterior relates to the site
The structure is hidden behind a neutral skin
n: Wright repeated materials, motifs, and basic ordering principles throughout, so the whole building works as a unified organism down to the furniture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: Organic architecture promotes harmony between what?
o: Human habitation and the natural world
n: Organic architecture seeks harmony between human habitation and nature, so buildings, furnishings, and surroundings form one composition.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: Which of these is NOT one of the Gaia Charter's rules for organic design?
o: Follow the historic style of the region
Unfold, like an organism, from the seed within
"Grow out of the site" and be unique
Carry the rhythm of music and the energy of dance
n: The Gaia Charter never asks designers to follow a historic regional style. Its rules include growing out of the site, unfolding from the seed within, and expressing music and dance.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: The Guggenheim summary says De Stijl was based on which geometry?
o: The straight line, square, and rectangle, with strong asymmetry
The circle and sphere, in strict symmetry
n: De Stijl rested on the straight line, square, and rectangle, combined with strong asymmetry and a play of positive and negative elements.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: What does 'De Stijl' mean, and by what other name is the movement known?
n: De Stijl is Dutch for 'The Style', and the movement is also called neoplasticism. 'New Art' is the meaning of Art Nouveau.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: Architect and planner David Pearson's rules for organic architecture are known as what?
n: Pearson's rules are the Gaia Charter. The Athens Charter is the CIAM town-planning document, and the Venice Charter concerns conservation.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: Who coined the term 'organic architecture'?
n: Frank Lloyd Wright coined the term, though his cryptic style of writing never fully articulated it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Organism

q: What is the Dutch term for 'neoplasticism', the new plastic art behind De Stijl?
n: Neoplasticism is Nieuwe Beelding. Nieuwe Zakelijkheid is 'New Objectivity', a different movement.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: In which essay did Mondrian set out the limits of neoplastic art?
n: Mondrian's essay is "Neo-Plasticism in Pictorial Art". 'Ornament and Crime' is by Adolf Loos, and the futurist manifesto by Marinetti.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: The Neo-Plasticism row of the isms table says De Stijl was founded in 1917 in which city?
n: The isms table says Amsterdam. The movements table on page 3 says Leiden, so the reviewer contradicts itself; answer from the table the question names.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 9 — Architectural Isms: Neo-Plasticism

q: What failing of CIAM-Functionalism did Structuralism respond to?
o: Its lifeless urban planning that ignored the identity of inhabitants and urban forms
n: Structuralists objected that functionalist planning had become a lifeless expression that ignored who lived there and the forms of the city.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Structuralism

q: A housing authority in England builds prefabricated low-cost units on low-value sites. Which ism describes this?
n: Utilitarianism refers to low-cost housing on low-value sites; in England it specifically means prefabricated units.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Utilitarianism

q: Radicalism is a shift from buildings of the past to designs that meet the demands of modern life. Who are named as its proponents?
n: Van de Velde and Gropius are the named proponents of Radicalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Radicalism

q: In the general sense, structuralism holds that elements of culture must be understood how?
o: Through how they fit into a bigger system that ties them together
n: Structuralism, found also in linguistics, anthropology, philosophy, and art, says cultural elements make sense only within an overarching system or structure.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Structuralism

q: Structuralism in architecture and urban planning arose around the middle of the 20th century as a reaction to what?
n: Structuralism reacted against CIAM-Functionalism, or Rationalism, whose urban planning had become lifeless and ignored the identity of inhabitants and urban forms.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Structuralism

q: Philosopher Simon Blackburn summarised structuralism as the belief that human phenomena are intelligible only through what?
n: Blackburn said phenomena of human life are intelligible only through their interrelations, which form a structure with constant laws of abstract culture behind local variations.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Structuralism

q: Which ism concerns itself with the nature of the house in the city, intricate designs for small houses, and the relationship between houses and society?
n: Post-Metabolism explains the house in the city through small-house designs and their relationship to society. Utilitarianism is about low-cost housing on cheap sites.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 10 — Architectural Isms: Post-Metabolism

q: How were Modernist plans typically arranged?
o: As cellular rooms off a central corridor
n: Modernist plans were loosely arranged, often open-plan.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: In Learning from Las Vegas, which kind of building uses signs to communicate its message?
n: The 'decorated shed' communicates through signs. The 'duck' puts its message into its sculptural structure.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: In Learning from Las Vegas (1972), what is a 'duck'?
o: A plain building that uses signs to communicate
A casino with an open plan
A sculptural building whose structure itself embodies its message
A building copied from a historical style
n: A 'duck' is a sculptural building whose form carries the message. The 'decorated shed' is the opposite, a plain building that relies on signs.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: Le Corbusier had a profound impact on which country after World War Two, through many public housing schemes?
n: The table singles out Le Corbusier's influence on post-war British public housing.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Which 1966 book by the American architect Robert Venturi was a key influence on Postmodernism?
n: Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) was the key influence. Learning from Las Vegas came later, in 1972.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: You are identifying a building that has rectangular, cubist shapes, almost no ornament, a reinforced concrete frame, large windows, and an open plan. Which ism is it?
n: Those are the Modernist things to look for. Brutalism also uses concrete, but with massive forms and small windows rather than large ones.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: By the 1970s, how had Modernism begun to seem, despite its democratic intentions?
n: Modernism had begun to seem elitist and exclusive, even though it meant to serve everyone.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: Modernism is also called the International Style, after an exhibition of modernist architecture in America. Who held it, and when?
n: Philip Johnson's 1932 exhibition gave the style the name International Style. His 1988 exhibition introduced Deconstructivism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Which ism threw out ornament for minimalism and went on to lead architecture and design worldwide in the 1900s?
n: Modernism rejected ornament and embraced minimalism to become the century's dominant movement. Postmodernism came later as a reaction against it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: What window arrangement often resulted from Modernism's metal and glass frameworks?
o: Small windows set deep in thick walls
n: Metal and glass frames allowed large windows in horizontal bands. Small windows in massive walls are a Brutalist trait.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Modernist buildings tended toward what exterior finish, often emphasised in black and white photography?
n: Modernism favoured white or cream render. Board-marked raw concrete is the Brutalist finish.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Modernism is associated with which approach to buildings?
o: Revival of historical styles with modern services
An analytical approach to function, rational use of materials, openness to structural innovation, and no ornament
Symbolic distortion of form for emotional effect
Growth of the building from its natural site
n: Modernism is tied to analysing function, using often new materials rationally, embracing structural innovation, and eliminating ornament. Distortion for emotional effect is Expressionism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Which of these is NOT a listed characteristic of Modernism?
o: Steep pitched roofs with decorative mouldings
n: Modernist buildings have flat roofs and no ornament or mouldings. Asymmetry and reinforced concrete are both on the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: A building uses classical motifs, literary allusions, bright colours, and a variety of materials and shapes. Which ism is it?
n: Classical motifs, literary allusions, bright colours, structural variety, and mixed materials are what to look for in Postmodernism. Neo-Plasticism also uses strong colour, but only primaries on straight lines.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: Postmodernism describes the colourful styles of architecture and decorative arts that appeared when, and in reaction to what?
o: The late 20th century, in reaction to Modernism
The early 20th century, in reaction to Art Nouveau
The mid-19th century, in reaction to Neoclassicism
n: Postmodernism appeared in the late 20th century as a reaction to Modernism and its dogmas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: In practice, what did the Postmodern approach produce?
o: An architecture of historical allusion with dashes of whimsy
An architecture of raw concrete masses
An architecture with no reference to the past
n: Postmodernism rediscovered the meanings in mainly classical architecture and applied them to modern structures, giving historical allusion and whimsy.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: Modernism is said to encompass several movements. Which is NOT one of them?
n: Modernism encompasses Futurism, Constructivism, De Stijl, and Bauhaus. Art Nouveau, with its rich ornament, came before and stands outside it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: The collapse of which tower block in 1968 exposed the failure of Modernist building methods and materials?
n: Ronan Point, a tower block in east London, collapsed in 1968. Pruitt-Igoe is a famous American failure, but it is not the one the table cites.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: In Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture, what did Venturi praise besides the ambiguities of Mannerist and Baroque Rome?
o: Popular culture and the ordinary architecture of the American Main Street
The grand scale of totalitarian buildings
n: Venturi celebrated popular culture and the ordinary architecture of Main Street, alongside the idiosyncrasies of Mannerist and Baroque Rome.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: In what year did Ronan Point, the east London tower block, collapse?
n: Ronan Point collapsed in 1968. 1966 and 1972 are the years of Venturi's two key books.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Post Modernism

q: In Britain, the term 'Modern Movement' described the rigorous Modernist designs of which period?
n: In Britain, 'Modern Movement' covered rigorous designs from the 1930s to the early 1960s. The 1950s to mid-1970s is Brutalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Which two architects are named as the leaders of Modernism?
o: Frank Lloyd Wright and Louis Sullivan
Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson
Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown
n: Gropius (1883–1969) and Le Corbusier (1887–1965) are named as leaders. Venturi is the key Postmodernist writer.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 11 — Architectural Isms: Modernism

q: Which of these is NOT listed as a trait of Art Nouveau?
n: Art Nouveau composition is asymmetrical, not symmetrical. Flowing lines, rich ornament, and colour and gilding are all on the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: What reason did the Nazi-led government give for its pressure on the Bauhaus?
o: That it was a centre of communist intellectualism
That it wasted public money on experiments
That it refused to train military engineers
n: The government claimed the Bauhaus was a centre of communist intellectualism. The Swiss Marxist director Hannes Meyer had made that charge easy to raise.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: What was Art Nouveau called in Italy?
n: The Italian name is Stile Liberty (the table writes "Modern Isme or Stile Liberte"). Coup de Fouet is Belgian and Style Nouille is French.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: What date range does the isms table give for Art Nouveau?
n: The isms table dates Art Nouveau 1890 to 1910. The same reviewer gives 1890–1914 in the style timeline and 1890–1920 in the movements table, so note which table a question draws on.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: Who directed the Bauhaus from 1928 to 1930, between Gropius and Mies van der Rohe?
n: Hannes Meyer directed the school from 1928 to 1930. Gropius led it from 1919 to 1928, and Mies from 1930 until it closed in 1933.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: In Austria, the Art Nouveau movement went by what name?
n: The Austrian version is the Sezession. Jugendstil is the German name, a common mix-up because both are German-speaking countries.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: The Bauhaus (1919 to 1933) is described as what?
o: A government housing agency of the Weimar Republic
A Russian avant-garde group serving the socialist regime
A creative centre of artistic experiment during the 1920s
n: The isms table calls the Bauhaus a creative centre of artistic experiment in the 1920s. The journal is De Stijl, and the Russian avant-garde is Constructivism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: Belgian Art Nouveau, known as the Coup de Fouet or 'whiplash' style, is tied to which architects?
n: Van de Velde and Horta are the Belgian pair; the table writes the name as "Coup-De-Joulet". Olbrich and Endell are listed with Van de Velde under German Jugendstil.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: How did the Bauhaus come to close in 1933?
o: It lost its funding when Gropius emigrated
It was merged into the New Bauhaus in Chicago
Its own leadership closed it under pressure from the Nazi government
Its Berlin building was destroyed in a fire
n: The leadership closed the school under pressure from the Nazi-led government, which claimed it was a centre of communist intellectualism. The New Bauhaus in Chicago was founded later by an émigré.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: For which years was the Bauhaus based in Dessau?
n: Dessau was home from 1925 to 1932, the longest of the three stays. 1919–1925 is Weimar and 1932–1933 is Berlin.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: In France, the Art Nouveau style was initiated by which designer?
n: Guimard initiated the French version, the Style Nouille (the table spells it "Style Nouville"). Horta and Van de Velde are the Belgian names.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: What was the Bauhaus founder's attitude toward interference from the German ruler?
o: Hannes Meyer welcomed state control of the curriculum
Mies van der Rohe moved the school abroad
Walter Gropius merged the school with a state academy
Walter Gropius would rather close the school than be dictated to
n: Gropius, the founder, would rather close shop than take dictation from the German ruler, which is how the school's end is framed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: Wavy, flower-based Art Nouveau ornament first took shape in which two countries near the close of the 1800s?
n: It developed in France and Belgium toward the end of the 19th century, then took local names elsewhere, such as Jugendstil in Germany and Sezession in Austria.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: German Jugendstil is tied to three designers in the table. Which name does NOT belong with them?
n: Van de Velde, Olbrich, and Endell are the Jugendstil names. Mackintosh represents Scotland.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: Which designer represents Art Nouveau in Scotland?
n: Mackintosh is the Scottish name. The table's label for the Scottish branch is garbled ("Fin-De-Schism"), but the designer is clear.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: In what order did the Bauhaus occupy its three German cities?
n: The school was in Weimar (1919–1925), Dessau (1925–1932), and Berlin (1932–1933).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Bauhaus

q: The American branch of Art Nouveau is named after which designer?
n: American Art Nouveau is the Tiffany Style, after Louis Tiffany. Sullivan used rich ornament too, but he is listed with the Chicago School and Functionalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: Art Nouveau emphasised the decorative and structural properties of which materials especially?
n: Glass and ironwork are singled out. Raw concrete belongs to Brutalism, and steel with plastics to high-tech.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: What was Art Nouveau called in Spain, and which architect is tied to it?
n: Spanish Art Nouveau was Modernismo, and Gaudí is its named architect. Stile Liberty is the Italian name and Sezession the Austrian.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Art Nouveau

q: Le Corbusier's 1953 Secretariat Building (Palace of Assembly), one of the best-known early Brutalist works, is in which city?
n: The Secretariat is in Chandigarh, India. His other famous early Brutalist work, the 1952 Unité d'Habitation, is in Marseilles.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: New Brutalism encouraged béton brut. What is béton brut, and how is its texture made?
o: Polished marble cut with diamond saws
Pre-cast panels with a smooth white finish
Raw concrete, with patterns from wooden shuttering replicated by board marking
n: Béton brut is raw concrete; the grain of the wooden formwork is left on the surface as board marking, as in Denys Lasdun's work.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: A building has massive concrete shapes that collide abruptly, with its service ducts and ventilation towers overtly displayed. Which ism is it?
n: Colliding concrete masses and exposed service towers describe Brutalism. Modernism kept a smooth white or cream render instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: How many European architects founded CIAM?
n: A group of 28 European architects founded CIAM. Seven is the number of architects in Philip Johnson's 1988 deconstructivist show.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: CIAM or International Modernism

q: The Hunstanton school that first earned the 'Brutalism' label was built mainly of what?
n: The table notes it was a steel building rather than reinforced concrete, which is surprising for a style now linked with raw concrete.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: What period does the isms table give for Brutalism?
n: Brutalism runs from the 1950s to the mid-1970s. The 1930s to the early 1960s is the British 'Modern Movement' listed under Modernism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Where was CIAM founded in June 1928?
o: The Château de la Sarraz in Switzerland
The Museum of Modern Art in New York
n: CIAM was founded at the Château de la Sarraz in Switzerland, by a group of 28 European architects.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: CIAM or International Modernism

q: CIAM, which ran from 1928 to 1959, was organised to do what?
o: Fund social housing after World War I
Spread the principles of the Modern Movement through congresses across Europe
n: The International Congresses of Modern Architecture held congresses to spread the Modern Movement's principles into landscape, urbanism, industrial design, and other domains.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: CIAM or International Modernism

q: Brutalism is described as 'architecture in the raw'. What does it emphasise?
o: Materials, textures, and construction, giving highly expressive forms
Ornament and gilding over a steel frame
n: Brutalism puts materials, textures, and construction on show to produce expressive forms. Historical motifs and bright colours are Postmodernist traits.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: What sets the 'brick brutalists' apart from other Brutalist architects?
o: They ruggedly combined detailed brickwork with concrete
They used brick only for interiors
n: Brick brutalists combined detailed brickwork with concrete. Brutalist buildings in general are massive and fortress-like, even when they are not large.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Brutalism is seen in Le Corbusier's work from the late 1940s, starting with which building?
n: The Unité d'Habitation in Marseilles marks the start. Villa Savoye (1931) is a white Early Modernist house, and the Chandigarh Secretariat came in 1953.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Which of these is NOT listed as a Brutalist trait?
o: Small windows in relation to the other parts
n: Horizontal bands of large windows belong to Modernism. Brutalist buildings have small windows compared with their massive forms.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Banham's term 'Brutalism' first referred to which building, notable for its uncompromising display of structure and services?
o: Alison and Peter Smithson's school at Hunstanton, Norfolk
n: It referred to the Smithsons' Hunstanton school, a steel building rather than reinforced concrete. Ronan Point is the collapsed tower block cited under Postmodernism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Which London development is cited for concrete whose aggregate was bush- or pick-hammered?
n: The Barbican Estate is the example of hammered aggregate. Lloyd's and the Waterloo Terminal are high-tech buildings.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: Which Filipino architect designed massive brutalist structures such as the Cultural Center of the Philippines and the Philippine International Convention Center?
n: Leandro Locsin designed both. Mañosa is known for a Filipino vernacular approach, and Antonio for Art Deco.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: The first line under Brutalism in the isms table refers to the works of which architect, with glass and steel and exposed service systems?
n: The table's opening line credits Van der Rohe's glass-and-steel works that display ducts, plumbing, and pipes. The rest of the row turns to raw concrete and Le Corbusier.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: CIAM was one of many 20th-century manifestos meant to advance what cause?
o: Architecture as a fine art for the elite
n: CIAM advanced "architecture as a social art", in line with the Modern Movement's aim to serve society broadly.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: CIAM or International Modernism

q: Who first used the term 'Brutalism' in England, and in what year?
n: The architectural historian Reyner Banham used the term in 1954. Giedion and 1928 belong to the founding of CIAM.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: Brutalism

q: CIAM's founding was organised by Le Corbusier, the castle owner Hélène de Mandrot, and which first secretary-general?
n: Sigfried Giedion was CIAM's first secretary-general. Banham came later, as the historian who named Brutalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 6 — Architectural Isms: CIAM or International Modernism

q: Which of these is NOT on the isms table's list of deconstructivist architects?
n: Moshe Safdie is listed with the Metabolists. The deconstructivists listed are Eisenman, Libeskind, Hadid, Gehry, and Koolhaas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: Constructivist architecture combined engineering and technology with what?
n: Constructivism joined engineering and technology to political ideology, with abstract geometric shapes and functional machine parts.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Deconstructivist ideas are borrowed from which French philosopher?
n: Jacques Derrida is the source of 'deconstruction'. The other three are French thinkers too, which is what makes them plausible.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: Constructivism spread outside the USSR by the late 1920s. Which movement then eclipsed it?
o: Art Deco in the United States
n: Within a few years Constructivism faded and was eclipsed by the Bauhaus in Germany, even though many European architects had called themselves constructivists.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: What is called the hallmark of deconstructivist architecture?
o: Its apparent instability, though it is structurally sound
n: Deconstructivist projects look like they are exploding or collapsing yet are structurally sound. The table stresses it is not an architecture of decay or demolition.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: How many architects did Philip Johnson gather for MoMA's 1988 'Deconstructivist Architecture' exhibit?
n: Johnson gathered works from seven architects. Twenty-eight is the number of architects who founded CIAM.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: What date range does the isms table give for Constructivism?
n: Constructivism is dated 1920 to 1930. 1928–1959 is CIAM, and 1917–1931 is the narrow span of De Stijl work.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: How did constructivist architects try to suggest humanity's collectivism?
o: Through classical temple fronts on public buildings
Through a harmonious arrangement of diverse structural elements
n: They used a harmonious arrangement of diverse structural elements to express collectivism, rather than applied imagery.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: The Russian avant-garde architects who called themselves constructivists held which core belief?
o: That buildings should grow like living organisms
That form should follow historical precedent
n: Constructivists believed design began with construction, and they worked for the new socialist regime. Growth like an organism is the idea behind Metabolism and organic architecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Tatlin's Tower, proposed in 1920 but never built, was meant as a monument to what?
o: The victory in World War I
The founding of the Soviet Union
n: It was a monument to the 3rd International, planned for St. Petersburg, then called Petrograd.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Which of these is NOT a trait of constructivist architecture?
o: Visible tech elements like antennae, signage, and screens
n: Floral ornament and gilding are Art Nouveau. Constructivism used glass and steel, machine-made parts, technological details, abstract geometry, and a sense of movement.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Inside the spirals of Tatlin's Tower, which three glass-walled units would rotate at different speeds?
o: A sphere, a cone, and a cube
A cube, a pyramid, and a cylinder
A cylinder, a dome, and a prism
A pyramid, a sphere, and a ring
n: A cube, a pyramid, and a cylinder were to rotate inside, while the spiral frame symbolised revolution and human interaction.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Deconstructivism, dated 1980 in the isms table, approaches architecture in what way?
o: As a unified organism growing from its site
As a return to classical order and proportion
In bits and pieces, with its basic elements dismantled
As a kit of prefabricated plug-in capsules
n: Deconstructivism views architecture in bits and pieces and dismantles its basic elements, so its buildings may seem to lack visual logic. Plug-in capsules are a Metabolist idea.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: The 1988 exhibit presented architects who, in the organiser's words, intentionally violate what?
o: The building codes of New York
The cubes and right angles of modernism
The rules of the Bauhaus curriculum
n: Johnson's architects "intentionally violate the cubes and right angles of modernism", which is the break the show was built around.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: Which values does deconstructivist architecture challenge, proposing that flaws are intrinsic to the structure?
n: Deconstructivism gains its force by challenging harmony, unity, and stability. 'Firmness, commodity, and delight' is the Vitruvian triad, a different idea.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: Tatlin's Tower would have soared how high, making it taller than the Eiffel Tower?
n: It was to rise about 400 m, or 1,300 ft. 381 m is the Empire State Building and 452 m the Petronas Towers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Which architect is NOT on the table's list of constructivists?
n: Erich Mendelsohn is an expressionist. Melnikov, El Lissitzky, and Chernikhov are all on the constructivist list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Which architect launched the Constructivist movement, and with what proposal?
o: El Lissitzky, with the Lenin Tribune
Konstantin Melnikov, with the Rusakov Club
Aleksandr Vesnin, with the Palace of Labour
n: Vladimir Tatlin launched Constructivism when he proposed his futuristic glass-and-steel tower. Melnikov and Vesnin are on the constructivist architects list, but not as its founder.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: What did the spiral forms of Tatlin's Tower symbolise?
o: The rise of the proletariat to heaven
n: The spirals stood for revolution and human interaction.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: In which city was Tatlin's Tower to be built?
n: The tower was planned for St. Petersburg, known in 1920 as Petrograd. Moscow is the usual wrong guess.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Three brothers appear on the list of constructivist architects: Aleksandr, Leonid, and Viktor. What is their surname?
n: Aleksandr, Leonid, and Viktor Vesnin are the three brothers on the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Constructivism

q: Deconstructivist architects rejected Postmodernist ways in favour of an approach closer to what?
n: Deconstructivism is described as more akin to Russian Constructivism, which it echoes in fragmented, dynamic geometry.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism

q: Which architect was NOT among the seven in the 1988 MoMA deconstructivist exhibit?
n: The seven were Eisenman, Gehry, Hadid, Koolhaas, Libeskind, Tschumi, and Coop Himmelblau. Renzo Piano is a high-tech architect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 7 — Architectural Isms: Deconstructivism
